questions.stem: An engineer asks: "Which files define classes that extend `BasePaymentHandler`?" Which built-in tool should the agent use first?

options.text: Grep, searching file contents for a pattern like `extends BasePaymentHandler`.
options.why: Grep searches inside files, which is what this question needs.

options.text: Glob with `**/*Payment*`.
options.why: Glob matches file paths. Subclasses may have any file name.

options.text: Read every file in `src/`.
options.why: This is hugely wasteful.

options.text: Bash running `ls -R`.
options.why: It lists names only.

questions.explanation: Grep searches file contents. Glob matches file paths and names.

questions.stem: The agent needs to find every Terraform file under any `modules/` directory. Which built-in tool fits best?

options.text: Glob with a pattern like `**/modules/**/*.tf`.
options.why: Path-pattern matching is what Glob is for.

options.text: Grep for the string `resource`.
options.why: This matches content, misses some files and includes unrelated ones.

options.text: Read on the `modules` directory.
options.why: Read reads files. It doesn't search by pattern.

options.text: Edit with an empty replacement.
options.why: That is nonsensical for search.

questions.explanation: Use Glob to match path patterns and Grep to search content.

questions.stem: The agent's Edit call fails because the `old_string` it chose (`return null;`) appears 14 times in the file. What should it do?

options.text: Retry Edit with a longer, unique anchor that includes surrounding context (for example the function signature and adjacent lines). If a unique anchor isn't feasible, Read the file and Write the full updated content.
options.why: Edit needs a unique match, and Read + Write is the fallback.

options.text: Replace all 14 occurrences.
options.why: That changes code that shouldn't change.

options.text: Use Bash `sed -i 's/return null;/return undefined;/'`.
options.why: This also replaces every occurrence and bypasses the safer edit tooling.

options.text: Give up and ask the engineer to edit manually.
options.why: There is a standard recovery path.

questions.explanation: Edit requires unique anchor text. Widen the context to make it unique, or fall back to Read + Write.

questions.stem: Even though a wiki MCP server is connected, the agent keeps running Grep over the local repo for questions like "what's our on-call policy?" (which is documented only in the wiki). What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Improve the wiki MCP tool's description so it states clearly that it searches internal policies, runbooks and process docs that aren't in the repo, with example queries.
options.why: Weak MCP tool descriptions lose to familiar built-in tools. Clear descriptions fix the selection.

options.text: Remove Grep from the agent.
options.why: Grep is essential for code questions.

options.text: Copy the wiki into the repo.
options.why: It goes stale immediately and duplicates the source of truth.

options.text: Set `tool_choice` to force the wiki tool on every turn.
options.why: This breaks code questions.

questions.explanation: Enhance MCP tool descriptions so the agent picks them over built-in tools when appropriate.

questions.stem: The team needs the agent to read and comment on GitHub issues. A developer proposes writing a custom MCP server. What is the better first option?

options.text: Use an established community or official GitHub MCP server, and build custom only for gaps specific to Halyard.
options.why: Prefer existing servers for standard integrations. Custom servers add maintenance burden.

options.text: Write the custom server, because it can be tuned exactly.
options.why: This is unnecessary build-and-maintain cost for a standard integration.

options.text: Give the agent Bash and let it call `curl` against the GitHub API.
options.why: This is less safe and less structured, and the agent has to handle auth ad hoc.

options.text: Paste issue contents into the chat by hand.
options.why: It doesn't scale.

questions.explanation: For standard integrations, prefer community MCP servers over building custom ones.

questions.stem: An engineer adds a new MCP server to the project config while an agent session is running, but the agent doesn't see the new tools. Why?

options.text: MCP tools are discovered when the client connects to the servers, so the session has to reconnect or restart to pick up the new server.
options.why: Tool discovery happens at connection time.

options.text: The new server must be listed in CLAUDE.md.
options.why: CLAUDE.md doesn't register MCP servers.

options.text: MCP servers can only be added at user scope.
options.why: Project scope (`.mcp.json`) is supported.

options.text: The agent's `tool_choice` must be `any`.
options.why: This has nothing to do with discovery.

questions.explanation: Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection time.

questions.stem: The `legacy/billing/` directory has unusual conventions (Java 8, no Lombok, a custom logging wrapper) that apply only within that directory tree. Where should those conventions go?

options.text: A CLAUDE.md inside `legacy/billing/`, which applies when working in that directory.
options.why: Directory-level memory suits conventions that follow the directory tree.

options.text: The root CLAUDE.md, so they're always available.
options.why: They would bloat every session's context and might be misapplied elsewhere.

options.text: User-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
options.why: That isn't shared with the team.

options.text: A skill that engineers must remember to invoke.
options.why: The conventions wouldn't apply automatically.

questions.explanation: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md suits conventions bounded by a directory. Path-glob rules suit scattered files.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between putting deployment-runbook knowledge into a skill and putting it into CLAUDE.md?

options.text: A skill loads on demand when it is relevant or invoked. CLAUDE.md content is loaded into every session.
options.why: This is the essential trade-off: on-demand versus always-on context.

options.text: Skills can't contain Markdown.
options.why: False. SKILL.md is Markdown with frontmatter.

options.text: CLAUDE.md can only hold coding-style rules.
options.why: False. It can hold any persistent instructions.

options.text: Skills are user-only and can't be shared.
options.why: Project skills in `.claude/skills/` are shared.

questions.explanation: Use CLAUDE.md for what must always apply and skills for specialised procedures that load on demand.

questions.stem: A `/db-migrate` skill should only be able to read files and run the migration CLI. It must never edit source code. Which SKILL.md frontmatter setting enforces this?

options.text: `allowed-tools`, listing only the permitted tools (for example `Read` and the specific Bash command pattern).
options.why: This restricts the skill's tool access.

options.text: `context: fork`
options.why: This isolates context. It doesn't restrict tools.

options.text: `argument-hint: <migration-name>`
options.why: This is only an argument hint.

options.text: A sentence in the skill body: "Do not edit files."
options.why: That is probabilistic. The frontmatter restriction is enforced.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` in SKILL.md frontmatter restricts which tools a skill may use, which follows least privilege.

questions.stem: An engineer gives Claude three review comments on its patch: (1) a function rename that affects (2) an interface change in the same module, and (3) an unrelated typo in a README. How should the feedback be delivered for the best result?

options.text: Send (1) and (2) together in one message, because they interact, and handle (3) separately.
options.why: Batch interacting issues together and handle independent ones sequentially.

options.text: Send all three one at a time in separate messages.
options.why: Splitting interacting changes risks inconsistent intermediate states.

options.text: Send all three plus any future feedback in one giant message.
options.why: Mixing independent issues dilutes focus.

options.text: Fix (3) yourself and ignore (1) and (2).
options.why: This doesn't address the review.

questions.explanation: Iterative refinement means grouping interdependent changes and sequencing independent ones.

questions.stem: An engineer wants Claude to build a CLI tool but has only a vague idea of the requirements. Which technique is most likely to produce the right tool?

options.text: The interview pattern: ask Claude to question the engineer about requirements, edge cases and constraints before writing any code.
options.why: It surfaces requirements that the engineer hasn't articulated.

options.text: Ask Claude to build the most feature-rich version possible.
options.why: This produces a bloated tool that still misses the real needs.

options.text: Start coding immediately and fix issues later.
options.why: It wastes iterations on the wrong problem.

options.text: Copy a similar tool from the internet.
options.why: That isn't tailored to the actual requirements.

questions.explanation: The interview pattern is a refinement technique for underspecified tasks.

questions.stem: An engineer asks the assistant to "find all places where we handle currency rounding and check they're consistent" across about 300 files. What is the best decomposition?

options.text: First map the relevant files (Grep for rounding call sites). Then analyse each file or module in focused local passes, and finish with a cross-file integration pass that compares the approaches.
options.why: Local passes plus an integration pass avoid attention dilution.

options.text: Load all 300 files into one prompt and ask for a consistency report.
options.why: Attention dilutes over huge inputs and context limits are exceeded.

options.text: Only check the five largest files.
options.why: This leaves coverage gaps.

options.text: Ask the engineer to list the files first.
options.why: The agent can map the files itself.

questions.explanation: For broad analysis, map the structure, do per-file local passes, then run an integration pass across files.

questions.stem: Some sessions produce runaway loops of 200+ tool calls, so the developer wants a safety mechanism. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Keep `stop_reason` as the primary loop control, and add a generous iteration or budget limit only as a safety net that surfaces an error or escalates when hit.
options.why: Caps are acceptable as a backstop, not as the primary termination mechanism.

options.text: Replace `stop_reason` handling with a hard cap of 10 iterations.
options.why: This truncates legitimate multi-step work. Using a cap as the primary stop is an anti-pattern.

options.text: Stop the loop when the model's text says "finished".
options.why: This relies on parsing natural language.

options.text: Remove tool access after 5 calls.
options.why: This is arbitrary and breaks complex tasks.

questions.explanation: Loop control relies on `stop_reason`. Limits are only safety nets with explicit handling.

questions.stem: The assistant must never run `kubectl delete` or `terraform destroy`, even if an engineer's prompt asks it to. What is the most reliable control?

options.text: A PreToolUse hook (or permission deny rule) that inspects Bash commands and blocks those patterns deterministically, returning an explanation to the agent.
options.why: Destructive actions need deterministic, code-level enforcement.

options.text: A system-prompt instruction to refuse destructive commands.
options.why: This is probabilistic and can be overridden by user pressure or prompt injection.

options.text: Ask the model to double-check before running any command.
options.why: The guarantee still depends on the model's judgement.

options.text: Log all commands and review them weekly.
options.why: This is detection after the damage is done.

questions.explanation: Use hooks and permission rules for hard guarantees. Prompts can only guide.

questions.stem: Engineers want the assistant to answer questions that span three areas: code, the issue tracker and deployment history. A developer proposes three specialised subagents behind a coordinator. When is this better than a single agent with all the tools?

options.text: When each area produces verbose intermediate work that would bloat one context, and each needs a focused toolset. Subagents isolate context and return concise findings to the coordinator.
options.why: Context isolation and focused toolsets are the main benefits of subagents.

options.text: Always, because more agents means better answers.
options.why: Multi-agent systems add latency and complexity, so they aren't always better.

options.text: Never, because subagents can't use MCP tools.
options.why: False.

options.text: Only when using the Batches API.
options.why: Unrelated.

questions.explanation: Choose multi-agent designs for context isolation, parallelism and scoped tools, not by default.

questions.stem: In a long debugging session the assistant has accumulated many large Bash outputs and file reads, and it starts contradicting earlier conclusions. Which TWO actions help most? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Record the confirmed findings in a scratchpad file, and reference that file instead of the raw outputs.
options.why: Durable, compact notes beat a long, noisy history.

options.text: Compact the conversation (for example `/compact`) or start a fresh session seeded with the summary.
options.why: This resets degraded context while keeping the essentials.

options.text: Re-run all the previous commands so the outputs are fresh.
options.why: This adds even more bloat.

options.text: Increase `max_tokens` on responses.
options.why: That affects output length, not context quality.

options.text: Switch on extended thinking for every turn.
options.why: It doesn't remove the bloated context causing the problem.

questions.explanation: Context degradation in long sessions is countered with scratchpads, compaction or summarisation, and fresh contexts.
